messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In these lines, Majeed does not appear openly cunning or apathetic. The quoted image—waking Bibi, carrying Jamila wrapped in a thin quilt, Rahima bewildered at his heels—suggests urgency, concern, and responsibility. If his earlier portrayal is cynical or self-interested, this moment complicates it: he is acting to protect, not to neglect.

But I would not call it pure deontological goodwill. The language is practical: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” This is not simply an abstract duty; it points to an intended outcome—safety, continuity, household stability, avoidance of worse consequences. In that sense, the action is teleological: its moral value comes from the result it produces. It may be framed as duty (he protects the women, he maintains his role), but the driving logic is calculation: securing a better consequence for himself and the family.

So the same traits are not obvious in the quoted lines themselves. His apathy is absent, and his cunning is not crude; it is subtler. The moment can be read as a deontological mask over a teleological motive: he does the right thing because it serves a useful end, not because good-will alone moves him.

Palindromes included: level, radar, civic, refer, madam, minim, rotor, racecar, repaper, reviver, rotator, tenet.
